article.title: Why Gross Margin Can Fall Even When Prices Rise
article.why: 拆解 price、cost、discount、mix 與 channel 對 gross margin 的共同影響。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Raising prices does not automatically improve gross margin. A company can charge more and still see its gross margin fall if costs, discounts, product mix, or channel mix move in the wrong direction.

Gross margin compares gross profit with revenue. If a product sells for 100 dollars and costs 60 dollars, gross profit is 40 dollars and gross margin is 40 percent. Now imagine the price rises to 105 dollars, but input costs rise to 70 dollars. Gross profit becomes 35 dollars and gross margin falls to about 33 percent. The higher price did not fully offset the cost increase.

Product mix can create another surprise. Suppose a company sells both premium products with high margins and basic products with low margins. If customers shift toward the basic line, total revenue may grow while average gross margin declines. The company may even raise prices across both lines and still report a lower overall margin.

Discounting matters as well. A list price increase looks positive, but if sales teams offer larger discounts to protect volume, the realized selling price may rise much less than expected. Analysts should therefore compare list price, average realized price, and discount rate rather than assume the announced increase reached the income statement.

Channel mix also affects economics. Direct sales may carry a higher margin than sales through distributors or marketplaces. If growth comes mainly from lower-margin channels, the blended gross margin can fall even when unit prices rise.

Currency and logistics can matter too. Import costs, freight, packaging, tariffs, and unfavorable exchange rates may increase cost of goods sold. These factors are easy to miss when managers focus only on the customer-facing price change.

A useful margin bridge separates the movement into price, volume, mix, and cost. It can show, for example, that price added two percentage points, product mix reduced one point, and raw-material costs reduced three points. That explanation is more useful than simply saying ‘margin fell despite a price increase.’

Managers should also distinguish gross margin percentage from gross profit dollars. A lower percentage can still produce more gross profit if volume grows strongly. Conversely, a higher percentage does not guarantee more profit if sales volume collapses.

The practical lesson is to treat price as one driver among several. When margin moves, ask what happened to realized price, unit cost, product mix, customer mix, discounting, and channel mix. The headline ‘we raised prices’ is not the conclusion. It is only one input into the explanation.

This decomposition is especially useful after a broad price revision. Rather than judging the program from one company-wide percentage, compare major products, customer groups, and sales channels. Different parts of the business may react differently. One segment may accept the higher price with little volume loss, while another may require heavy discounts. Looking at the components prevents a blended average from hiding those differences.

Timing also matters. Costs and prices may change in different months. A company might announce a price increase in April, but existing contracts may delay the benefit until July, while raw-material costs rise immediately. In that case, margin can worsen temporarily even if the pricing action is economically sensible. Analysts should therefore map the effective date of price changes against the timing of cost changes and contract renewals.

The best discussion is not ‘Did price go up?’ but ‘How much of the price increase was realized, what costs moved at the same time, and which mix changes helped or hurt?’ That framing turns a simple percentage into an explanation of business economics.
paragraphs.zh: 漲價不代表毛利率一定提高。真正結果同時受單位成本、折扣、商品組合、通路組合與價格實現時點影響。分析時最好做 price-volume-mix-cost bridge，並區分毛利率與毛利額。
paragraphs.ja: 値上げしても粗利率が必ず改善するわけではありません。原価、値引き、商品ミックス、チャネル構成、価格反映時期まで分解して見る必要があります。

quiz.question: Why can gross margin fall after a price increase?
quiz.answer: Because costs, discounts, or mix can worsen by more than the realized price improves.
